title: Geroscience & Regenerative Biology
description: Mechanisms linking aging biology to tissue resilience, damage response, senescence, stem-cell function, and regeneration—taught with evidence appraisal and translational caution.

modifications: 2026-10-07: added four original lessons (survival and healthspan endpoints; senescent-cell causality; clonal hematopoiesis and circulating factors; aging clocks and partial reprogramming) beside the preserved legacy units; retagged the four legacy checks to the objectives they assess.

prerequisites.statement: Cell biology; Genetics; Biochemistry; Biostatistics recommended

outcomes.description: Distinguish organismal aging mechanisms from correlates.
Interpret senescence and stem-cell assays with controls.
Evaluate causal evidence for an intervention.
Separate lifespan, healthspan, and tissue-function endpoints.

lesson_objectives.description: Compare damage, maintenance, and adaptation models.
Distinguish biomarker change from improved function.
Define senescence operationally using multiple features.
Distinguish cell-state evidence from a single marker.
Relate stem-cell function to niche signals and tissue demand.
Distinguish cell number from self-renewal and differentiation capacity.
Evaluate whether an intervention's mechanism is supported by its endpoints.
Design a study that separates efficacy from toxicity or selection effects.
Calculate an interval death probability and a Gompertz mortality-rate doubling time from cohort data.
Distinguish lifespan, healthspan, and tissue-function endpoints, including the effects of censoring and survivor selection.
Evaluate whether a lifespan study's design supports the generality of its claim.
Compare genetic and pharmacologic senescent-cell clearance designs and state what each can establish.
Calculate intention-to-treat and survivor-only response estimates and explain how treatment-related dropout biases efficacy.
Identify mechanism-linked senolytic toxicities and select measurements that would detect them.
Explain clonal expansion in an aging stem-cell pool and convert a variant allele fraction into an estimated clone size.
Evaluate heterochronic parabiosis and blood-exchange designs, separating dilution of old-blood factors from supply of young-blood factors.
Identify assay-specificity and replication problems in claims about single circulating factors.
Explain how epigenetic clocks are trained and calculate age acceleration as a residual from a reference calibration.
Evaluate whether a clock change supports rejuvenation, considering noise, cell composition, regression to the mean, and identity loss.
Design measurements for a partial-reprogramming experiment that separate youthful features from dedifferentiation and tumor risk.

lessons.title: Aging as a systems process
lessons.worked_example: A change in an epigenetic clock after intervention does not by itself show that tissue function or healthspan improved; both should be measured independently.

lessons.title: Survival curves, mortality hazards, and healthspan endpoints
lessons.worked_example: If monthly hazard rises from 0.010 at 18 months to 0.040 at 30 months, G = ln 4/12 ≈ 0.116 per month and the mortality-rate doubling time is about 6.0 months. A group with half the hazard at every age keeps the same doubling time yet lives longer, so doubling time and median lifespan answer different questions.

lessons.title: Senescence, inflammation, and tissue context
lessons.worked_example: A senescence-associated β-galactosidase-positive cell is not conclusive alone; a panel plus evidence of persistent arrest and appropriate controls is stronger.

lessons.title: Clearance models, senolytics, and dropout-aware efficacy
lessons.worked_example: With 40 animals per arm, 19 of 38 vehicle survivors and 20 of 32 senolytic survivors improved, an apparent 12.5-point benefit. Counting the deaths as not improved gives 47.5% versus 50.0%, a 2.5-point difference: treatment-related deaths removed animals unlikely to improve, so survivors alone overstate benefit.

modules.title: Stem cells, niches, and regenerative capacity

lessons.title: Stem cells, niches, and regenerative capacity
lessons.worked_example: An expanded progenitor population after injury may reflect compensatory proliferation; it does not establish durable self-renewal or restoration of organ function.

modules.title: Aging stem-cell pools and circulating factors

lessons.title: Clonal hematopoiesis and circulating-factor claims
lessons.worked_example: If 72 of 800 reads carry a DNMT3A variant, the variant allele fraction is 0.09. For a heterozygous autosomal mutation without copy-number change, about 2 × 0.09 = 18% of sampled nucleated cells carry it; a binomial standard error near 0.010 already makes 0.07–0.11 plausible.

lessons.title: Intervention evidence and translational design
lessons.worked_example: If a senolytic improves function only in animals that tolerate a high dose, reporting survivors alone can exaggerate benefit; intent-to-treat and toxicity analyses are essential.

lessons.title: Aging clocks and partial-reprogramming rejuvenation claims
lessons.worked_example: With a calibration clock age = 4 + 0.92 × chronological age, a 50-year-old reading 55 has age acceleration 55 − 50 = +5 years, while an 80-year-old reading 80 has +2.4 years despite a raw difference of zero. Selecting people for high acceleration guarantees some decline on retest, so a randomized control is required.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added four original lessons with explicitly synthetic data tables, worked examples, 15 formative items, 16 retrieval cards, and 21 link-only scientific references: survival curves, Gompertz hazards and healthspan endpoints; genetic and pharmacologic senescent-cell clearance with dropout-aware efficacy; clonal hematopoiesis and circulating-factor claims; and epigenetic clocks with partial reprogramming. Mapped every lesson objective to a course outcome and retagged the four legacy checks to the objectives they assess. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

limitations: Four compact legacy units are preserved beside four original substantial lessons; this package is not equivalent to a full university semester.
There is no authored 12–15 week schedule, substantive homework sequence, laboratory sequence, midterm, cumulative final, or graded integrative project.
Formative checks cover each new lesson's objectives, but the first objective of each legacy unit still has no tagged practice item; this is not demonstrated comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery.
Bloom labels, objective-to-outcome links, and structured prerequisite edges are authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
All data tables in the new lessons are synthetic teaching data; cited studies are summarized qualitatively from link-only references and are not reproduced.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.
Numerical items use unitless answers with stated tolerances; significant-figure and dimensional checks have not been authored for this package.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.
intentionally_omitted: A full instructional sequence, graded assessments, and laboratory activities are not authored yet; the new lessons extend a partial package.
No dosing, treatment, supplement, or clinical-test recommendations are given; intervention content is limited to evidence appraisal.
